title: Joining Masonry and the musicians in the lodge
summary: Caldwell was a mason from 1946; Lem Johnson, the deacon of the blues, and others advanced through the degrees.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: But -- well now, we're into the -- now, you returned to New York in 1945 from Philly.
Now, this is about the time you get into Masonry.

It seems to me we're just going to get onto this next tape, and I think it would be just a nice thing if you told about the musicians that were in your lodge and what you know, I mean of the effect maybe that has on their lives.
Some of them, of course, I suppose join and then sort of fall away, just like members of a

Some do, yeah. Good, now the majority of fellows like Lem Johnson, called the deacon of the blues, and Lem, when I was master, he was my junior warden, but you work around the chairs. You work your way up. And they all join the consistory which you get to 32nd degree in the consistory because Shriners (15) not a symbolic body of masonry anyway. It's just something set aside that the people know (unintelligible) might want us -- different house, but you should -- generally these children call it the Playhouse.

But when you go up there, you got to have money. So lot of people don't go (unintelligible) Scottish Rites. Scottish Rites, there's two ways to go up to 32nd, either York Rite or the Scottish Rite. Well, all of us went Scottish Rite way, to get to 32nd. However, we all (unintelligible) myself Harry Dial Dial Lem (unintelligible), Larry Dow -- before Dow -- and we all did our lectures, worked around, go to the East. Well, actually about the highest honor you can get in (unintelligible) Masonry, become a master of the blue house.
Suppose you stop there. The tape's going to run out.
